blocks.title: Overlap work without violating when values become available
paragraphs: A pipeline overlaps stages from different instructions. Latency measures the time for one instruction; throughput measures the completion rate after filling. Overlap does not remove dependencies or resource conflicts.

The teaching workspace uses five equal stages F,D,X,M,W, single in-order issue, separate stage resources and no branches. Fetch waits before a dependent instruction when needed. Register writeback may be read in D in the same cycle. These are explicit model rules, not claims about every physical CPU.

blocks.title: Count filling, steady issue and stalls
paragraphs: With k stages and n instructions, issuing one instruction per cycle without stalls takes k+n−1 cycles from the first stage of the first instruction through the last stage of the last instruction. Four instructions through five stages therefore take eight cycles.

Three additional stall cycles make that total eleven. If each stage cycle is 2 ns, ideal instruction latency is 10 ns and ideal steady-state throughput is one completion per 2 ns; four ideal instructions finish in 16 ns. Do not multiply n by full latency once overlap is allowed.

blocks.title: A dependency is not always a stall
paragraphs: A read-after-write dependency requires the consumer to receive the producer’s new value. Forwarding can send a result directly to a later stage without waiting for architectural register writeback. A result must already exist at the receiving stage’s required time.

In this model an ALU result is ready after X, and a load result after M. A directly following ALU consumer can use ALU forwarding without a stall, while a directly following load consumer needs one stall. Without forwarding, wait until the producer’s W cycle for the consumer’s D read.

Structural hazards arise from competing resource uses. Control hazards arise because the next instruction depends on a branch decision; misprediction can discard speculative work. Branch penalty must be stated, not inferred from the presence of a branch.

blocks.title: Construct the controlled dependency schedule
paragraphs: The workspace sequence is ALU A; ALU B depending on A; independent Load C; ALU D depending on C. With forwarding, F start cycles are 1,2,3,5. Adding stage offsets 0,1,2,3,4 gives the completion of D at cycle 9, with one inserted wait.

Without forwarding, starts are 1,4,5,8: B reads in D at cycle 5 when A writes back, and D reads at cycle 9 when C writes back. The last W is cycle 12. Do not assume forwarding eliminates a load-use dependency before memory data is ready.

blocks.title: Schedule around dependencies, not around appearances
paragraphs: List each instruction’s producers, result-ready stage and resource needs. Place instructions in a candidate schedule, then check every use against availability and every shared resource against capacity.

Moving independent work into a delay slot may reduce stalls, but reordering must preserve dependencies and required effects. Multiple schedules can be correct; compare them using the stated machine and cost criterion.

For a separate stated branch model, add non-overlapping penalties explicitly. For example, two mispredictions each costing three cycles add six cycles; do not double-count cycles already counted as another stall.

blocks.title: State the machine before the timing claim
paragraphs: Separate latency, throughput, filling/draining and stalls. Derive producer-to-consumer timing and inspect the complete schedule.
Practice and the workspace use explicit models. Open instruction reordering is an unscored structured self-check, not a single-layout answer key.

cards.prompt: Why is an ideal k-stage pipeline time k+n−1 cycles for n instructions?
cards.answer: The first instruction needs k stages; each of the remaining n−1 instructions completes one cycle later under single-issue, no-stall assumptions.

cards.prompt: Does pipelining reduce one instruction’s latency to one stage?
cards.answer: No. It overlaps different instructions. One instruction still passes through all stages; steady throughput can improve without reducing its latency.

cards.prompt: Why can load-use still stall with forwarding?
cards.answer: A load’s value is not ready until the declared memory stage completes. Forwarding cannot deliver a result before it exists.
The specified branch-resolution/prediction and recovery rules. Count only the actual non-overlapping lost cycles, not an assumed universal penalty.

cards.prompt: How do you check a proposed instruction schedule?
cards.answer: Check every producer/consumer availability time, each resource’s capacity and preservation of program effects. Then count the final completion cycle.

cards.prompt: May independent-looking instructions always be reordered?
cards.answer: No. Establish all data, memory and control dependencies and required effects first. Multiple safe schedules may exist under the stated model.

guided.title: Compare schedules without enforcing one drawing
guided.prompt: Explain how moving an independent instruction between a load and its consumer could help, and identify the conditions that make the change safe.
rubric: Show that the consumer’s required value is available later than the immediately following use would allow.
Verify that the moved work does not depend on or change required data/memory/control effects.
Rebuild the timing under the declared resources/forwarding rules. Accept any schedule satisfying those constraints; no arbitrary reference layout is scored.
